issues.item: Avoid Social Contacts: Seeing people that I socialised with before the event
issues.explanation: The Maladaptive Strategies node mixes avoidance behaviours with what appears to be a trigger-like cue. 'Seeing people that I socialised with before the event' is phrased as a social reminder/trigger rather than a coping strategy, so within the specified node it is clinically incoherent.

issues.item: Avoid Intimacy: Being emotionally close or intimate with others
issues.explanation: 'Avoid Social Contacts' and 'Avoid Intimacy' imply social withdrawal, which can fit PTSD, but the specific target 'seeing people that I socialised with before the event' suggests avoidance of trauma reminders tied to the past. This sits awkwardly with the selected Negative Appraisals, which focus on incapacity, moral injury, and not belonging, without any corresponding interpersonal mistrust, shame in relationships, or reminder-based social threat theme.

issues.item: Belong Nowhere: I no longer belong anywhere
issues.explanation: 'Belong Nowhere: I no longer belong anywhere' is possible in PTSD, but here it leans toward a broad identity/interpersonal alienation theme that is not well supported by the rest of the profile. The Threat items are predominantly hypervigilant safety-checking and pursuit fears, while the other appraisal items emphasize incapacity and violated values; this makes the belonging item feel disconnected rather than part of a coherent appraisal cluster.

vignette:
Kiet Phommachanh is a 26-year-old Lao-American man who works as a bank teller at a mid-sized regional branch in a suburban strip mall. He was referred for psychological services by his employee assistance program following a terrorism-related incident approximately fourteen months ago, in which a coordinated attack targeted a crowded public market near his apartment during a weekend visit to a neighboring city. Kiet had gone there with his then-wife to pick up groceries and visit a vendor they knew. The attack unfolded without warning - an explosion, then screaming, then the particular quality of chaos that no prior experience had prepared him for. In the immediate aftermath, Kiet made a decision he has not been able to set down since: rather than staying to help the people around him, he ran. He pulled away from his wife's grip in the crowd and moved toward an exit. He has described this moment in session with a flatness that suggests he has replayed it thousands of times without resolution. His wife was unharmed. Their marriage did not survive the following year.

In the weeks after the attack, Kiet began to notice that he was not the same person he had been. He had always thought of himself as someone others could count on - steady, composed, the kind of person who stayed calm in a crisis. That self-understanding collapsed entirely. He had come to believe, with a certainty that felt irrefutable, that he had revealed something permanent and disqualifying about himself on that afternoon. He was not capable. He could not be trusted - not by others, and not by himself. The man who had coached his younger brothers through difficult times, who had taken pride in being reliable, now felt like a fiction he had once performed convincingly.

At work, Kiet began arriving earlier and staying later. The branch opens at nine; he is typically there by seven-fifteen. He volunteers for every additional shift, covers colleagues' absences without being asked, and fills his lunch breaks with administrative tasks he could complete at any other time. His manager has noted his dedication in performance reviews, unaware that the teller window and the procedural rhythm of transaction processing are, for Kiet, less about professional ambition than about the alternative - the silence of his apartment, where his thoughts have room to move. When the branch finally closes and he has no more tasks to manufacture, the evenings are difficult. He tries hard not to think about the market, about the grip he broke, about what he believes his running means about him. The effort of suppression is visible in sessions as a kind of muscular vigilance - a jaw that tightens when certain words are spoken, a subject changed with practiced efficiency.

His nights are disrupted. He wakes in the early hours, often between two and four in the morning, and lies still for a moment before moving through his apartment to check the locks, the windows, the back entrance. He does not fully understand why this feels necessary; he only knows that sleep without it does not feel available to him. At work, he frequently turns to look behind him when customers are queuing, particularly when the branch is busy and the ambient noise rises. He has become short-tempered in ways that surprise him - a colleague's abrupt question, a customer who lingers too long at the window, and Kiet feels a heat rise in him that he does not recognize as his own.

His divorce was finalized six months ago. He has not pursued any close relationships since, and when colleagues have invited him to social events, he has declined. Emotional proximity feels, to him, like exposure to something he cannot afford. What finally brought him to seek help was not the sleeplessness or the anger, but a moment at the teller window last month when a customer thanked him warmly for his patience and he felt nothing - not pleasure, not recognition, nothing. He sat in his car afterward and understood, perhaps for the first time, that whatever he had been managing was not working. What he hopes for is modest and painful in its specificity: he wants, he said quietly in the intake session, to be someone he can count on again.
